title: DNSSEC unsigned: what it actually means for radblok.co.za
summary: The whois record for radblok.co.za showed DNSSEC: unsigned. Dug into what that actually means — how DNS cache poisoning works, what an attacker can do once a resolver is poisoned, why HTTPS only partially saves you, and how DNSSEC closes the gap with a chain of cryptographic signatures from the root down to my zone.

blocks.text: When someone types `radblok.co.za` into a browser, their device asks a **recursive resolver** (ISP's, or 8.8.8.8, or 1.1.1.1) to figure out the IP. The resolver does a chain of lookups:

items: Ask a root nameserver → "ask ZARC for .co.za"
Ask ZARC's nameserver → "ask ns1.host-h.net for radblok.co.za"
**Cache that answer for TTL seconds**, serve it to the client — and every other client who asks

blocks.text: The critical word is **cache**. The resolver stores that answer and reuses it for every client until the TTL expires. And there is **zero authentication** in this chain. The resolver has no way to verify the answer is genuine. It just trusts whoever responded.

sections.h: DNS cache poisoning — the actual attack (Kaminsky, 2008)

blocks.text: The attacker's goal: get a fake answer into the resolver's cache before the real one arrives. DNS runs over UDP — there's no handshake. A response just needs to carry the right transaction ID to be accepted. The resolver can't tell a fake from a real answer if the ID matches.

blocks.label: attack flow
blocks.text:
# Attacker sends resolver a flood of fake UDP responses
# each claiming to be from ns1.host-h.net
# each with a different transaction ID, racing to match

# If one fake response lands before the real one:
#   → resolver caches the fake IP for radblok.co.za
#   → every client asking gets the attacker's server
#   → lasts until the TTL expires — could be hours

Modern resolvers randomise source ports too (you now have to guess port AND transaction ID), but it's still a probabilistic attack — harder, not impossible. And on a network where the attacker has any MITM position (a rogue AP, a compromised router, a BGP hijack), they don't even need to race — they can just intercept and replace the response directly.

sections.h: What the attacker can do once the cache is poisoned

blocks.text: Any client whose resolver has the poisoned cache entry is now talking to the attacker's server instead of mine. What they can do with that:

head: Target
Attack
Blocked by HTTPS?
rows: Web traffic
Serve a clone site, harvest credentials
Partially — browser cert warning if attacker has no cert
First HTTP visit
Intercept before HTTPS upgrade fires
No — HSTS only helps after the first visit
Email (MX records)
Poison MX → intercept inbound mail to @radblok.co.za
No — mail routing has no cert check at the DNS level
New visitors
No HSTS preload for my domain → first visit is HTTP
No
CA cert issuance
Some CAs verify domain control via DNS — poisoned DNS = fraudulent cert
No — defeats HTTPS entirely

blocks.text: The email angle is the most underrated. HTTPS protects web traffic. It does nothing for SMTP routing. A poisoned MX record redirects inbound mail silently — no browser, no warning, no cert check.
DNSSEC adds **cryptographic signatures** to every DNS record in the zone. xneelo would sign them with a private key held in the zone:

blocks.label: signed zone (simplified)
blocks.text:
radblok.co.za  A      X.X.X.X
radblok.co.za  RRSIG  (signature over the A record, signed with zone key)
radblok.co.za  MX     mail.radblok.co.za
radblok.co.za  RRSIG  (signature over the MX record)
ZARC signs a **DS record** (a hash of my zone's public key) and publishes it in the .co.za zone. The root signs ZARC's key. This creates a **chain of trust**:

blocks.label: chain of trust
blocks.text:
Root (.) → signs ZARC's key
  ZARC (.co.za) → signs my zone key
    My zone (radblok.co.za) → signs every record

A DNSSEC-validating resolver checks the whole chain when it gets an answer. If a poisoned or fake answer arrives, **the signature won't verify** — the resolver rejects it and returns `SERVFAIL` instead of serving the bad data. The attack is blocked at the resolver level, before it ever reaches the client.

sections.h: Unsigned vs signed: the concrete difference

head: Scenario
DNSSEC unsigned (now)
DNSSEC signed (fixed)
rows: Attacker poisons 8.8.8.8 cache
8.8.8.8 has no signature to check → caches fake answer → serves it to everyone
8.8.8.8 checks signature → mismatch → SERVFAIL → attack blocked
Attacker intercepts MX record
Mail routing silently redirects to attacker
Signature check fails → resolver refuses the fake MX
CA issues fraudulent cert
Nothing at DNS level stops it
CAA record (also signed) restricts which CAs can issue → misissuance blocked

sections.h: Why HTTPS only partially saves you

items: **HTTP-first traffic** — any redirect from HTTP to HTTPS hits the attacker's server before the upgrade fires. On that first request, you're already exposed.

**No HSTS preload** — HSTS (the header that forces HTTPS on future visits) only kicks in after the first successful HTTPS visit. A brand-new visitor to `radblok.co.za` has no preload. First visit with a poisoned resolver = attacker's server, no warning.
**Email (MX)** — HTTPS protects web traffic. SMTP routing is DNS-based with no equivalent cert check. A poisoned MX record redirects inbound mail silently.

**CA misissuance** — CAs sometimes verify domain ownership via DNS or HTTP challenge. Poisoned DNS can make a CA think the attacker controls the domain, resulting in a legitimate cert for the attacker. HTTPS then shows a green padlock on a malicious site.

sections.h: How to fix it on radblok.co.za

items: Log in to xneelo's control panel.
Enable DNSSEC — xneelo generates the zone signing key (ZSK) and key signing key (KSK), signs all records.
xneelo submits the **DS record** (hash of your KSK) up to ZARC.
ZARC publishes the DS record in the `.co.za` zone — chain of trust is complete.

blocks.label: kali — verify after enabling
blocks.text:
# Check for RRSIG records (signatures on your A record)
$ dig radblok.co.za A +dnssec
# Should see RRSIG records next to the A record
# and 'ad' flag (authenticated data) in the response header

# Check the DS record at ZARC level
$ dig radblok.co.za DS +trace

Takes 5 minutes to enable in the control panel, up to 48 hours to propagate through the DNS hierarchy. Cost: free. While you're there, also add a **CAA record** — it tells CAs that only xneelo is authorised to issue TLS certs for radblok.co.za, closing the misissuance angle too.

items: Understood DNS cache poisoning — the Kaminsky attack and why unsigned zones are vulnerable.
Mapped out exactly what an attacker can do with a poisoned cache: web cloning, mail interception, fraudulent cert issuance.
Understood why HTTPS only partially mitigates: HTTP-first traffic, no HSTS preload for new visitors, MX records unprotected.
DNSSEC fix: chain of trust from root → ZARC → zone key → signed records. Resolver rejects anything with a missing or bad signature.
**Action item:** enable DNSSEC on radblok.co.za via xneelo control panel. Also add a CAA record.
